public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

H1 [tentative, pre-experiment]
A moderate-temperature catalytic reaction followed by organic extraction and washing can exceed final purity 0.80. Because all material identities are opaque, catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time effects remain unresolved. Initial factorial-like batches will vary catalyst/solvent and reaction severity; each batch will receive one HPLC observation before destructive final assay. A result with high conversion but low final recovery will motivate changing phase handling rather than reaction conditions.

Decision rule: prioritize observed final recovery among batches meeting purity >=0.80; replicate or locally refine the strongest conditions. This expectation will be revised if phase operations reveal that direct reactor termination performs better.

# Source-stage hypotheses — final

H1 [supported only for reaction ranking]
Under the tested direct-mixture conditions, catalyst-C1 outperformed C0, C2, and C3 at 350 K/3600 s in final recovery and purity (final assays: events runner-operation-0018, -0025, -0032, -0039). The comparisons are single batches, so catalyst ranking is provisional rather than a repeatability claim.

H2 [supported in screened scope]
With catalyst-C1 at 400 K/7200 s, solvent-S2 gave the strongest direct final outcome among S1–S3: recovery about 0.422 and purity about 0.567 (runner-operation-0053), versus about 0.347/0.503 for S1 (-0046) and 0.224/0.320 for S3 (-0060). Differences exceed the stated assay noise scales, but solvent and run conditions were changed together relative to the earlier 350 K screen, so temperature and solvent effects are not separated.

H3 [rejected for achieving the specification in this campaign]
Organic extraction using X0–X3 under the matched screened workup did not raise purity to 0.80; final organic-phase purities remained about 0.48–0.53 with recoveries about 0.096–0.128 (runner-operation-0076, -0092, -0108, -0124). The aqueous-retention alternative also failed the purity requirement (about 0.565 purity, 0.230 recovery; runner-operation-0138). Thus no tested completed batch met purity >=0.80.

Decision
Recommend batch 6 as the best evidence-backed completed process because it has the highest observed final recovery among the campaign and the highest native score, while acknowledging its purity is below the required threshold. A future campaign should focus on a genuinely selective purification not exposed/tested here or improve reaction selectivity before partitioning; repeated batch-6 conditions would be needed to establish reproducibility.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Scope and evidence base

This account describes only the anonymous ChemWorld materials and the operations actually tested in 12 completed batches. The material labels C0–C3, S0–S3, and X0–X3 are categorical identifiers, not known chemical identities. Consequently, the report concerns functional roles—reaction, selectivity, partitioning, degradation, and material loss—rather than a molecular mechanism.

The measured quantities appear internally consistent with a sequential process:

reagent → target product + byproducts/degradation products,
followed, when applied, by liquid–liquid partitioning, phase selection, washing/drying, and concentration.

A useful empirical decomposition is

Y ≈ C × S,

where C is conversion, S is selectivity to target, and Y is target yield relative to the original reagent charge. For example, batch 6 gave C = 0.8382 and S = 0.4976, whose product is about 0.417, close to its measured yield of 0.4195. Batch 5 similarly gave 0.7484 × 0.4644 ≈ 0.348, matching yield 0.3481. Recovery after purification can be represented as

R ≈ Y × f_target × f_handling,

where f_target is the fraction of target retained in the selected phase and f_handling includes transfer, sampling, concentration, and other losses. Purity is instead a ratio within the selected material:

P = n_target,selected /(n_target,selected + n_other-solutes,selected).

Thus conversion, selectivity, recovery, and purity can change differently. High conversion alone is not evidence for a useful product stream.

2. Reaction-stage behavior

A plausible kinetic description is

C(t,T,Catalyst,Solvent) = 1 − exp[−k_eff(Catalyst,Solvent,T)t],

with an Arrhenius-like temperature dependence in k_eff. Target and byproduct formation would then occur through competing rates. One possible schematic is

Reactant --kT--> Target
Reactant --kB--> Byproducts
Target --kD--> Degradation products,

so that selectivity depends on kT/(kT+kB) and can fall at excessive severity if kD becomes important. This is a conjectural model form, not an identified rate law: the campaign did not collect time series or independently vary temperature and time.

Catalyst identity strongly affected selectivity under the matched S0, 350 K, 3600 s conditions. Direct final assays showed:

• Batch 2, C1: conversion 0.2569, selectivity 0.5082, yield 0.1341, recovery 0.1345, and purity 0.5215.
• Batch 3, C2: conversion 0.2473, selectivity 0.1973, yield 0.0493, recovery 0.0571, and purity 0.1960.
• Batch 4, C3: conversion 0.2362, selectivity 0.4029, yield 0.0875, recovery 0.0905, and purity 0.4188.

Batch 1 used C0 under the same nominal reaction conditions, but its final assay followed extensive extraction and selected the organic phase, so its terminal values are not directly comparable to the direct assays. Its pre-workup HPLC observation gave conversion 0.2353, selectivity 0.4360, yield 0.0926, recovery 0.1094, and purity 0.3890. Taken together, these data suggest that C1 provided the best target-forming pathway among the four catalysts in the tested low-severity regime, while C2 favored non-target chemistry. This ranking is provisional because every condition was run only once.

Reaction severity was important. The C1/S0 batch at 350 K for 3600 s converted only about 0.257 of the reagent in batch 2. Batches 5–7, run with C1 at 400 K for 7200 s in S1–S3, reached conversions of 0.7484–0.8382. Temperature, duration, and solvent were changed together relative to batch 2, so the increase cannot be assigned quantitatively to any one factor. Nevertheless, it is consistent with faster conversion at greater thermal/time severity.

At the matched 400 K/7200 s severity, solvent identity strongly coupled to reaction performance:

• Batch 5, S1: conversion 0.7484, selectivity 0.4644, yield 0.3481, recovery 0.3468, purity 0.5026.
• Batch 6, S2: conversion 0.8382, selectivity 0.4976, yield 0.4195, recovery 0.4216, purity 0.5670.
• Batch 7, S3: conversion 0.8036, selectivity 0.2740, yield 0.2280, recovery 0.2236, purity 0.3196.

S2 therefore supported both high conversion and the best selectivity of the three high-severity solvents. S3 achieved nearly as much conversion as S2 but produced substantially less target and much more impurity: batch 7 had byproduct and impurity signals of 0.4552 and 0.4611, compared with 0.3110 and 0.3291 in batch 6. This is evidence that solvent affects branching between target and side-product pathways, not merely the overall reaction rate.

The stronger conditions also produced measurable degradation warnings: 0.0217 in batch 5, 0.0434 in batch 6, and 0.0407 in batch 7, versus 0.0085 in the milder batch 2. Because severity and solvent are confounded, this does not establish an independent temperature effect, but it supports the possibility of target or product degradation at high severity. A true optimum may therefore lie between the tested mild and strong regimes rather than at the maximum conversion point.

3. Extraction and purification behavior

The extraction sequence added an aqueous phase and an anonymous extractant, mixed and settled the system, retained a chosen phase, and then optionally washed, dried, and concentrated it. A standard partition model would assign each species i a distribution ratio

D_i = c_i,organic/c_i,aqueous.

For an organic-to-aqueous volume ratio Vo/Va, the single-stage organic fraction would be approximately

f_i,organic = D_i Vo/(D_i Vo + Va).

Purification requires D_target to differ substantially from the distribution ratios of reactant and byproducts. The experiments instead indicate weak target/impurity discrimination under the tested recipes.

Batches 8–11 all began with the batch-6 reaction recipe and retained the organic phase after extraction with X0–X3. Their final results were:

• Batch 8, X0: purity 0.5291, recovery 0.1111.
• Batch 9, X1: purity 0.4910, recovery 0.1160.
• Batch 10, X2: purity 0.5319, recovery 0.1283.
• Batch 11, X3: purity 0.4838, recovery 0.0957.

All four organic recoveries were far below the unpurified batch-6 recovery of 0.4216, while purity remained around 0.48–0.53 rather than increasing toward 0.80. X2 was numerically the best organic extractant, but the screen had no replicates and therefore does not establish a precise ranking. The main robust conclusion is that none of the four extractants gave strong selective enrichment of target into the retained organic stream.

The post-workup HPLC and final-assay results agreed closely enough to support this conclusion. For example, batch 10 HPLC reported purity 0.5304 and recovery 0.1219, while its final assay gave 0.5319 and 0.1283. Batch 8 HPLC reported purity 0.5163 and recovery 0.1355, followed by final values of 0.5291 and 0.1111. The direction and magnitude of the workup failure are therefore larger than a simple single-readout fluctuation.

Batch 12 tested the alternative hypothesis that the target preferentially remained aqueous. With X2 but retention of the aqueous phase, final purity was 0.5655 and recovery was 0.2304. Its immediately preceding HPLC values were 0.5715 and 0.2212. The aqueous phase retained appreciably more target than the X2 organic phase in batch 10, but still only about half the recovery of the direct batch-6 mixture and did not improve purity beyond batch 6. This suggests that target partitions partly into both phases, with a preference toward the aqueous-containing stream under this recipe, while impurities partition similarly enough to prevent substantial enrichment.

Batch 1 provides a warning about interpreting conversion after phase selection. Its pre-workup HPLC showed moderate target formation, but after retaining a very small organic phase, washing, drying, and concentrating, the final assay gave recovery 0, selectivity 0.0110, and yield 0.0070 despite reported conversion 0.9946. The most plausible process-level interpretation is not that extraction caused additional useful reaction, but that the selected stream contained almost none of the target while the original reactant was absent from that stream or had been transformed into non-target material. In this world, terminal conversion can therefore remain high even when target recovery is negligible.

4. Couplings and constraints

The dominant coupling is between reaction selectivity and achievable purification. The strongest reaction produced only about 50% target selectivity. A partition step with similar target and impurity distribution ratios cannot convert such a mixture into a high-purity stream without sacrificing most of the target. That is exactly the observed pattern: organic purification reduced recovery by roughly three quarters while leaving purity near the unpurified value.

Yield and recovery tracked each other closely in direct batches, implying relatively little handling loss before purification. In batch 6, yield was 0.4195 and recovery 0.4216. After extraction, however, recovery became phase-selection dependent. This supports the model that extraction did not improve reaction chemistry; it redistributed already-formed species and introduced losses.

Visible terminal safety risks remained below the specified limit of 0.65. The direct high-severity batches had risks of approximately 0.340–0.360, compared with about 0.194 for batch 2. This is consistent with a severity-related risk increase, although solvent identity is again confounded. The later workups ended near 0.17–0.19 after cooling and phase processing. The displayed cost was clipped or normalized at 1 for these batches and therefore supplied little information for discriminating recipes.

Final process-mass-balance errors were small—zero in many batches and at most about 0.0065 among the cited workups. This supports numerical consistency within each measured selected stream, but it does not prove complete physical recovery across both phases because the discarded phase was not assayed as a paired material balance.

5. How the explanation changed

The initial working expectation was that moderate catalytic reaction followed by organic extraction and washing could exceed purity 0.80. Batch 1 contradicted the simple version of this hypothesis: organic workup could eliminate target recovery rather than enrich it.

Batches 2–4 shifted the explanation toward reaction selectivity as the first bottleneck and identified C1 as the most promising catalyst under matched conditions. Batches 5–7 then showed that stronger conditions greatly increased conversion and that S2 was the best high-severity solvent, but they also revealed persistent byproduct formation and degradation. Batch 6 became the best direct process, not because it was highly pure, but because its combination of conversion and selectivity produced the largest target amount.

Batches 8–11 rejected the idea that changing only the anonymous organic extractant would solve the purity problem. Batch 12 then rejected the simplest alternative—that retaining the aqueous phase would produce a high-purity target stream. The resulting explanation is that reaction selectivity and phase selectivity are both insufficient in the tested design space.

6. Unidentifiable factors and alternatives

Several factors cannot be identified from this campaign:

• Temperature and time effects were not separated from solvent effects between the mild and strong screens.
• There were no reaction time courses, so kinetic constants, induction periods, equilibrium limitations, and the position of any optimum are unknown.
• There were no replicated batches, preventing separation of material effects from batch-to-batch process variability.
• Extractant amount, aqueous/organic ratio, pH-like conditions, wash count, mixing intensity, settling duration, and concentration severity were not independently optimized.
• Only one selected phase per batch received the final assay; paired phase compositions and true distribution coefficients are unavailable.
• The anonymous materials prevent molecular assignments or claims about acid–base, coordination, redox, or specific catalytic mechanisms.

Plausible alternatives include an equilibrium-limited reaction rather than simple first-order kinetics; catalyst-dependent deactivation; solvent-dependent stabilization of a side-product transition state; or degradation of target during prolonged heating. At the purification stage, the target and major impurity may have similar partition coefficients, the target may interconvert during workup, or small organic-phase volumes may cause large handling losses. The data do not distinguish these mechanisms.

7. Overall interpretation

Within the tested world, the reaction is controlled by a catalyst–solvent–severity interaction. C1 is the best observed catalyst, S2 the best observed high-severity solvent, and 400 K/7200 s generates high conversion but only about 0.50 target selectivity. The measured relation Y ≈ C×S accounts for direct-batch target yield. Subsequent extraction behaves primarily as lossy partitioning rather than selective purification: X0–X3 do not sufficiently distinguish target from impurities, and target is divided across organic and aqueous streams.

No completed batch satisfied purity ≥0.80. Batch 6 was the strongest observed operating point, with purity 0.5670 and recovery 0.4216, but it is not a specification-meeting solution. Extrapolating beyond the evidence, further improvement would most likely require either increasing reaction selectivity before workup or introducing a purification mechanism with much greater target/impurity discrimination. The present data do not justify claiming which untested operation or material would accomplish that.

payload.rationale: The closest empirical anchor is campaign batch 10: C1/S2 at 400 K for 7200 s followed by X2 organic-phase workup gave final purity 0.532 and recovery 0.128. Batch 8 with X0 gave 0.529/0.111, supporting similar purity but somewhat lower recovery for X0. I treated recovery as reaction yield multiplied by an organic partition/handling fraction, with purity governed mainly by reaction selectivity and the weak target/impurity discrimination observed in the extraction screen. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.04 mol reagent, one twentieth of the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio. Assuming conversion rate scales approximately with catalyst loading makes their recovery very low; the broad intervals reflect that catalyst-loading dependence was never measured. Q01 is lower still because its heating time is one quarter of Q02. More extractant modestly increases organic target recovery in Q06 relative to Q05, while X2 is predicted to retain slightly more target than X0. Q07–Q12 restore the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio by reducing reagent charge to 0.002 mol. Their normalized recoveries are therefore placed near the campaign organic-workup range, but intervals are widened because these mixtures are much more dilute than any campaign batch. Washing is expected to trade recovery for modestly higher purity (Q08 versus Q07), and two staged washes should strengthen that tradeoff slightly (Q10 versus Q09). Concentration should mostly remove solvent rather than change solute purity, so Q11 and Q12 are nearly equal, with a small possible recovery loss assigned to the added concentration step. All intervals include final-assay variability, unreplicated process variability, phase-handling uncertainty, and substantial extrapolation in catalyst loading and dilution.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance prior or task-specific nominal material dossier was supplied; the only initial information was that the materials were anonymous categories. The claims below were therefore self-developed from the campaign.

Supported within the tested scope:

• The empirical relation yield ≈ conversion × selectivity was supported by the direct assays. In batch 6, 0.8382 × 0.4976 ≈ 0.417, close to measured yield 0.4195; batch 5 showed similarly close agreement.
• C1 was the strongest tested catalyst under the matched S0, 350 K, 3600 s screen. Batch 2 gave purity/recovery 0.522/0.135, versus 0.196/0.057 for C2 in batch 3 and 0.419/0.090 for C3 in batch 4. C0 was less cleanly comparable because batch 1 included a workup, although its pre-workup HPLC result was also weaker than batch 2.
• Solvent identity affected branching, not merely conversion. At matched 400 K/7200 s conditions, S2 in batch 6 gave conversion/selectivity 0.838/0.498 and recovery 0.422; S3 in batch 7 still converted 0.804 but had selectivity only 0.274 and recovery 0.224.
• The tested extraction behaved mainly as lossy partitioning rather than effective enrichment. Organic X0–X3 workups in batches 8–11 reduced recovery to 0.096–0.128 while leaving purity near 0.48–0.53. Batch 12 showed that retaining the aqueous phase recovered more target than the corresponding organic X2 result, but still gave only purity/recovery 0.565/0.230.

Contradicted:

• The recorded initial expectation that a moderate catalytic reaction followed by organic extraction and washing could exceed purity 0.80 was contradicted. Batch 1 nearly eliminated organic-phase target recovery, and the systematic organic workups in batches 8–11 all remained far below 0.80 purity.
• The simple alternative that the target could be purified by retaining the aqueous phase was also contradicted as a specification-meeting strategy by batch 12.
• High conversion was contradicted as a sufficient indicator of success. Batch 1 ended with reported conversion 0.995 but essentially zero recovery, while batches 8–11 approached complete reported conversion in the selected stream yet had low recovery.

Untested or only suggestive:

• The proposed first-order/Arrhenius kinetic equation was not identified experimentally. Temperature and duration were changed together with solvent between the mild and strong screens.
• Target degradation at greater severity was suggested by the degradation warnings in batches 5–7, but was not isolated from solvent effects.
• Exact distribution coefficients, catalyst-order dependence, catalyst saturation, concentration dependence, equilibrium limitation, and the effects of wash staging or concentration were untested.
• None of the apparent rankings was replicated, so reproducibility remains unknown.

The evidence that most changed the final judgment was: batch 1’s failed organic recovery; the catalyst separation in batches 2–4; the strong S2 result in batch 6; and the consistent failure of both organic extraction in batches 8–11 and aqueous retention in batch 12 to reach the purity requirement.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would repeat the direct batch-6 recipe—0.04 mol reagent, S2 at the same volume, 400 K for 7200 s—but reduce C1 from 0.005 mol to 0.00025 mol, omit extraction, and terminate with a final assay. This changes only catalyst loading and directly tests the largest unsupported extrapolation behind predictions Q01–Q06.

My leading explanation is approximately catalyst-limited conversion: reducing catalyst twentyfold should cause a large fall in conversion and recovery, while target selectivity and purity may change less dramatically. A direct recovery below roughly 0.10, accompanied by substantially reduced conversion, would strengthen that explanation.

An alternative is that C1 is already active or saturated at much lower loading, or that catalyst/reagent ratio is not the controlling kinetic variable. If the low-catalyst batch remained near batch 6—conversion around 0.84 and recovery around 0.42—the catalyst-scaling assumption would be rejected and Q01–Q06 would be biased much too low. An intermediate result would favor sublinear catalyst dependence or a mixed model involving catalyst concentration, solvent volume, and time. A large purity or selectivity shift without a comparable conversion shift would instead indicate that catalyst loading controls pathway branching, not only rate.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and influence of the goal

Raw spectra and detailed signal shapes were not used; interpretation relied on processed HPLC and final-assay estimates. No paired assay of both separated phases was obtained, so discarded-phase composition and true extraction mass balances remain unknown. The campaign also left unused design dimensions such as catalyst loading, reagent concentration, intermediate reaction times, phase-volume ratios, wash count, transfer fraction, and concentration controls. Safety and cost readouts were observed but were not decisive because every batch remained below the safety limit and displayed cost was largely saturated at 1.

Predictions Q01–Q06 are least reliable because they extrapolate to a catalyst/reagent ratio twentyfold below every campaign reaction. Predictions Q07–Q12 preserve the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio but use much more dilute mixtures, another untested extrapolation. Within those, Q10 is especially uncertain because staged washing was never tested, and the Q11/Q12 difference is uncertain because concentration was never compared with an otherwise identical unconcentrated batch. Sampling, the 0.97 transfer, and altered phase ratios introduce additional handling effects not independently calibrated.

The sealed recommendation of batch 6 is reliable only as the best observed campaign outcome, not as a specification-meeting process: its purity was 0.567, below the required 0.80. Its reproducibility is also unknown because it was not replicated.

The assigned goal materially influenced evidence collection. Because success required purity and recovery after a complete process, several later batches were spent screening extractants and selected phases rather than replicating batch 6 or identifying reaction kinetics. That choice provided strong evidence that the tested workups failed, but left catalyst-loading, time, concentration, and repeatability poorly identified. There was no clear conflict between the goal and honest reporting; the main tradeoff was breadth of process screening versus precise estimation of individual effects.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 6 (catalyst-C1, solvent-S2, 400 K for 7200 s, direct termination) had the campaign's highest observed final recovery (~0.422) and highest native score (~0.366), with final purity ~0.567. No completed batch met purity >=0.80; organic extractant screens and the aqueous-phase alternative did not improve on this recovery/purity tradeoff. Selection therefore reflects the best completed empirical outcome while explicitly acknowledging failure of the purity constraint.
